# Improving the Ingredient Parser

Mealie uses Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) for parsing and processing ingredients. The model used for ingredients is based off a data set of over 100,000 ingredients from a dataset compiled by the New York Times. I believe that the model used is sufficient enough to handle most of the ingredients, therefore, more data to train the model won't necessarily help improve the model.

## Improving The CRF Parser

To improve results with the model, you'll likely need to focus on improving the tokenization and parsing of the original string to aid the model in determine what the ingredient is. Data science is not my forte, but I have done some tokenization to improve the model. You can find that code under `/mealie/services/parser_services/crfpp` along with some other utility functions to aid in the tokenization and processing of ingredient strings.

The best way to test on improving the parser is to register additional test cases in  `/mealie/tests/unit_tests/test_crfpp_parser.py` and run the test after making changes to the tokenizer. Note that the test cases DO NOT run in the CI environment, therefore you will need to have CRF++ installed on your machine. If you're using a Mac the easiest way to do this is through brew.

When submitting a PR to improve the parser it is important to provide your test cases, the problem you were trying to solve, and the results of the changes you made. As the tests don't run in CI, not providing these details may delay your PR from being merged.

## Alternative Parsers
Alternatively, you can register a new parser by fulfilling the `ABCIngredientParser` interface. Satisfying this single method interface allows us to register additional parsing strategies at runtime and gives the user several options when trying to parse a recipe.


## Links
- [Pretrained Model](https://github.com/mealie-recipes/mealie-nlp-model)
- [CRF++ (Forked)](https://github.com/hay-kot/crfpp)

from fastapi import APIRouter

from mealie.routes._base import BaseUserController, controller
from mealie.schema.recipe import ParsedIngredient
from mealie.schema.recipe.recipe_ingredient import IngredientRequest, IngredientsRequest
from mealie.services.parser_services import get_parser

router = APIRouter(prefix="/parser")


@controller(router)
class IngredientParserController(BaseUserController):
    @router.post("/ingredient", response_model=ParsedIngredient)
    async def parse_ingredient(self, ingredient: IngredientRequest):
        parser = get_parser(ingredient.parser, self.group_id, self.session, self.translator)
        response = await parser.parse([ingredient.ingredient])
        return response[0]

    @router.post("/ingredients", response_model=list[ParsedIngredient])
    async def parse_ingredients(self, ingredients: IngredientsRequest):
        parser = get_parser(ingredients.parser, self.group_id, self.session, self.translator)
        return await parser.parse(ingredients.ingredients)

content.text:
To add a new parsing strategy, you change three places in the backend. The API routes themselves don't need edits.

**What must change**

1. **The parser class.** Write a new subclass of `ABCIngredientParser` (`mealie/services/parser_services/_base.py:130`). It must implement two abstract methods: `async parse_one(ingredient_string) -> ParsedIngredient` and `async parse(ingredients: list[str]) -> list[ParsedIngredient]`. The base `__init__` takes `group_id`, `session` and `translator`. It also gives you `repos`, the fuzzy-match thresholds, and `find_ingredient_match`, which swaps parsed foods and units for database matches. The existing parsers `BruteForceParser`, `NLPParser` and `OpenAIParser` (`mealie/services/parser_services/openai/parser.py`) are the models to follow.
2. **The enum.** Add a member to `RegisteredParser` (`mealie/schema/recipe/recipe_ingredient.py:519`). It currently has `nlp`, `brute` and `openai`. This enum is the `parser` field on `IngredientRequest` and `IngredientsRequest`, so adding a member is what makes the strategy selectable and validated in the API. It also shows up in the OpenAPI schema.
3. **The factory.** Register the class in `get_parser`, in `mealie/services/parser_services/ingredient_parser.py:318`. Normally you add an entry to the private `__registrar` dict, which maps `nlp` to `NLPParser` and `brute` to `BruteForceParser`. `openai` is special-cased with a lazy import. Use that pattern if your parser has heavy or optional dependencies. Any value that isn't in the registrar silently falls back to `NLPParser`, so a missing registration won't raise an error.

**What is affected**

- `IngredientParserController.parse_ingredient` and `parse_ingredients` in `mealie/routes/parser/ingredient_parser.py` are the only callers of `get_parser`. They pass `ingredient.parser` straight through, so they need no change.
- The `parser` field on the request schemas changes, so API clients and generated types are affected.
- I did not check the frontend. If its parser dropdown or generated TypeScript types list the enum values, they will need updating too.
- I did not check the existing tests, but you will want to add some for the new parser.

**What the docs say**

The contributor guide, under "Alternative Parsers", says to register a new parser by fulfilling the `ABCIngredientParser` interface. It says this lets additional strategies be registered at runtime and gives users several options when parsing a recipe.

The docs call it a "single method interface", but the code has two abstract methods. Follow the code.

The guide's CRF section is about improving the existing NLP parser, not adding a new one. It points to `mealie/services/parser_services/crfpp` and `test_crfpp_parser.py`. It also says those tests don't run in CI because CRF++ must be installed locally.

The AI providers page mentions that the AI parser is chosen as an alternative to the NLP and Brute Force parsers while parsing ingredients.

3. **The factory.** Register the class in `get_parser`, in `mealie/services/parser_services/ingredient_parser.py:318`. Normally you add an entry to the private `__registrar` dict, which maps `nlp` to `NLPParser` and `brute` to `BruteForceParser`. `openai` is special-cased with a lazy import. Use that pattern if your parser has heavy or optional dependencies. Any value that isn't in the registrar silently falls back to `NLPParser`, so a missing registration won't raise an error.

**What is affected**

- `IngredientParserController.parse_ingredient` and `parse_ingredients` in `mealie/routes/parser/ingredient_parser.py` are the only callers of `get_parser`. They pass `ingredient.parser` straight through, so they need no change.
- The `parser` field on the request schemas changes, so API clients and generated types are affected.
- I did not check the frontend. If its parser dropdown or generated TypeScript types list the enum values, they will need updating too.
- I did not check the existing tests, but you will want to add some for the new parser.

**What the docs say**

The contributor guide, under "Alternative Parsers", says to register a new parser by fulfilling the `ABCIngredientParser` interface. It says this lets additional strategies be registered at runtime and gives users several options when parsing a recipe.

The docs call it a "single method interface", but the code has two abstract methods. Follow the code.

The guide's CRF section is about improving the existing NLP parser, not adding a new one. It points to `mealie/services/parser_services/crfpp` and `test_crfpp_parser.py`. It also says those tests don't run in CI because CRF++ must be installed locally.

The AI providers page mentions that the AI parser is chosen as an alternative to the NLP and Brute Force parsers while parsing ingredients.
